title: Price Against the Market, Not Just the Customer
documentTitle: How Should AQ Think About Pricing? 2018 Holistic Pricing Context
excerptForBlog:
I read through this with some interest and have a naive question that you might advise me to discuss in person: all of the discussion on advertisers' reactions to our pricing changes seem to presume that this is a 2-person game between the advertiser and Google and — at some point on the pricing curve — advertisers could abandon us even if it behooved them to stick with us. But isn't it really 3 players — the advertisers, us, and our competitors? The discussion seems insensitive to where else the advertiser could obtain traffic of similar quality and price. Why is it ok to ignore this — isn't the real point where an advertiser switches us out determined by the surrounding market?

The underlying document frames the concern clearly: pricing on google.com happens today in small touches throughout the year, through what it terms 'incidental' pricing (quality and format improvements with CPC or CPA components) and 'intentional' pricing (auction mechanism tunings via format pricing, squashing, or reserves). The result is pricing happening in a 'semi-controlled, semi-organic way that might not be ideal.' Leadership expressed discomfort with intentional pricing launches, worried that cumulative changes could leave advertisers unhappy and cause them to reallocate budgets to other channels on timeframes Google cannot track. Two risk types are identified: advertisers lowering bids to restore ROI (manageable), and advertisers shifting spend away from Google permanently due to degraded sentiment — characterized as the more problematic outcome.

lessonTitle: Price Against the Market, Not Just the Customer
pullQuote: If your pricing model only has two players in it, you've already mispriced — the third player is the door your customer can walk through.
leadershipTraits: challenges the frame, not just the numbers
focused on what can't be measured
situation: In a memo dated January 1, 2019, Google executive Prabhakar Raghavan responded to an internal pricing document titled 'How Should AQ Think About Pricing? 2018 Holistic Pricing Context.' The underlying document described Google's ad pricing as happening in a 'semi-controlled, semi-organic way' through a mix of intentional and incidental mechanisms. Raghavan's note identifies a structural gap in that analysis: the competitive outside option is missing entirely.
insight: Raghavan's central challenge is precise. The internal pricing model, he writes, assumes 'a 2-person game between the advertiser and Google.' He argues it's actually three players — advertiser, Google, and competitors — and that the real defection point is 'determined by the surrounding market.' This is Porter's switching-cost logic applied in reverse: the document had been measuring advertiser pain tolerance in isolation, without anchoring it to what alternatives exist at what price and quality. The document also flags two distinct risk types: advertisers lowering bids to restore ROI (described as 'manageable') versus advertisers permanently shifting spend due to degraded sentiment. That second risk — silent, slow budget reallocation to other channels 'on timeframes Google cannot track' — is the one Raghavan flags as more dangerous. The pricing architecture creates a blind spot: you don't see the slow bleed until it's already happened.
application: When you model pricing changes, always build a column for the competitor alternative. For each customer segment, ask: what is the next-best option, and at what price does your offer stop winning? If your pricing analysis doesn't include that answer, you're measuring the wrong thing. Run this exercise before any intentional price move, not after you've already noticed budget erosion.
